package_info.package_versions: Variants A and B (May 2023, at least three variants)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is designed to encrypt user files, display fake system update screens, demand ransom for decryption, and exfiltrate ransom payments. It masquerades as legitimate software (e.g., fake Windows Update, fake Microsoft Word document), manipulates user trust, and disrupts system operations for extortion.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on execution of the malware binary)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Display a fake Windows Update screen for ~30 seconds, then encrypt files with randomly altered filenames.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C# (MSIL, based on AV signatures and Windows platform)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code displays a fake Windows Update UI to distract the user, then recursively encrypts files on the system, renaming them with random values, resulting in data loss and extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Displaying a fake system update is a classic social engineering tactic to distract users while malicious actions occur in the background. File encryption and renaming are hallmarks of ransomware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software updates do not encrypt user files or alter filenames. System updates should be signed and managed by the OS, not by third-party executables.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate system updates may display progress screens, but never encrypt user files.

execution_context.file_location: Main executable (variant A and B), dropped ransom note files

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drop ransom note file named 'README_[random seven digits]' or 'Read Me First!/txt' and set desktop wallpaper to ransom note image.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After file encryption, the code writes a ransom note to the filesystem and changes the desktop wallpaper to display extortion instructions, coercing the victim to contact the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping ransom notes and altering the desktop wallpaper are direct indicators of ransomware activity, intended to pressure the victim into paying.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not demand ransom or alter user desktop settings without consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may change wallpapers (e.g., customization tools), but not in conjunction with ransom demands.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PowerShell script 'cry.ps1' invoked to perform file encryption.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware drops and executes a PowerShell script that recursively encrypts files on the system, resulting in data loss and extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing a PowerShell script for file encryption is a common ransomware technique, leveraging built-in scripting to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not drop or execute encryption scripts without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PowerShell scripts are used for automation, but not for unauthorized file encryption.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (variant B, after ransom note creation)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attempt to open attacker's Github page in the default web browser.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After displaying the ransom note, the code attempts to open a URL (attacker's Github page) in the victim's default browser, possibly for further instructions or to track infections.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Opening an attacker's web page post-infection is a method to direct victims to payment or support channels, or to track successful infections.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not open arbitrary web pages without user consent, especially not attacker-controlled pages.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some installers open product pages post-install, but not in the context of extortion.
key_indicators: Automatic browser launch to attacker-controlled URL

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Encrypt files and append attacker's contact email (e.g., 'poop69new@[redacted]') to filenames.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code encrypts files and renames them to include the attacker's email address, facilitating victim identification and extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Appending an attacker's email to encrypted files is a direct indicator of ransomware, used to coerce victims into contact.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not alter filenames to include contact information for extortion.

attack_chain.action: User executes the malicious file (disguised as a Windows Update or Microsoft Word document).
Malware displays a fake Windows Update screen to distract the user.
Malware encrypts files on the system, renaming them (sometimes with attacker's email).
Malware drops ransom note files and changes the desktop wallpaper to display ransom instructions.
Malware attempts to open the attacker's Github page in the victim's browser.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential further instructions or infection tracking

behavioral_signatures: Display of fake Windows Update or other system dialogs during execution
Mass file encryption and renaming (including random values or attacker email)
Dropping ransom note files with unique naming patterns (e.g., README_[random digits], Read Me First!/txt, read_it.txt)
Changing desktop wallpaper to a ransom note image
Dropping and executing PowerShell scripts for file encryption
Automatic opening of attacker-controlled URLs post-infection
file_indicators: Wallpaper image files with ransom note content
network_indicators: Attempted access to attacker's Github page or other URLs included in ransom notes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for processes that display fake system update dialogs, perform mass file encryption/renaming, drop ransom note files with suspicious naming patterns, or change the desktop wallpaper unexpectedly. Watch for dropped or executed PowerShell scripts (e.g., cry.ps1) and for processes that attempt to open attacker-controlled URLs in the browser. File access patterns involving rapid, recursive modification and renaming of user files are strong indicators. Correlate with known file hashes and AV signatures for Big Head ransomware variants.
